title: Thinking in Conditions
summary: Build a mental model of conditional branching: evaluating boolean expressions to dynamically control program execution paths.
learningObjectives: Develop a boolean mental model for program decision making
Connect relational comparisons from Module 03 to conditional execution guards
Understand single-branch if execution: executing code when true and skipping when false
Visualize program branching using execution flowcharts
expectedOutcomes: Translate real-world business constraints into clean boolean expressions
Control console program execution paths dynamically without unconditional fall-through

activities.title: Decision Making & Boolean Flow in Java

breakdown.whatIsIt: Evaluating boolean conditions to selectively execute or skip blocks of statements.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Without conditions, programs can only perform fixed calculations without responding to dynamic state.
howItWorks: if evaluates the condition in parentheses to true or false.
If true, the enclosed block executes.
If false, the block is completely bypassed.
Conditions in Java must evaluate to strict boolean types (never integers).
keyTakeaways: An if block acts as a conditional gate in your code.
Java requires a strict boolean inside if (...); numbers like 0 or 1 cause compile errors.
Statements following the if block execute regardless of whether the branch was taken.
Relational comparisons (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=) form the foundation of conditional logic.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Speed Radar Warning
activities.description: Run this program with speed = 95, then speed = 70. Notice how the alert block executes when speed > 80, but is completely bypassed when speed is within the limit.

questions.prompt: What data type must the expression inside an if statement evaluate to in Java?
questions.explanation: Java enforces strict type safety: conditions in if statements must evaluate to boolean. Unlike C/C++, integers (0 or 1) cause a compile-time type mismatch.
hints: Java requires strict boolean truth values.

questions.prompt: What happens if the condition in an if statement evaluates to false?
options: The program halts with an exception
The block inside the if statement is skipped, and execution resumes immediately after it
Java checks the condition again in a loop
questions.explanation: When the condition is false, the body of the if block is bypassed completely, and control transfers to the next statement outside the block.
hints: It simply skips the code inside the curly braces.

questions.explanation: x > 15 evaluates to 10 > 15 (false). The block printing 'A' is skipped. Execution continues to the next statement, printing 'B'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following will cause a compilation error in Java?
questions.explanation: Writing 'if (1)' fails to compile in Java with 'Type mismatch: cannot convert int to boolean'. Only boolean expressions are valid conditions.
hints: Check which condition is an integer rather than a boolean.

questions.prompt: What condition correctly tests whether an integer 'val' is a positive non-zero number?
questions.explanation: Positive non-zero numbers are strictly greater than 0: 'val > 0'. (val >= 0 includes 0, which is neither positive nor negative).
'isVip = true' is an assignment operator (=), NOT an equality check (==)! It assigns true to isVip and evaluates to true! Thus the if block runs, printing 'VIP Guest'. Always use == for comparison!
hints: Notice the single '=' assignment operator inside the if condition.

questions.prompt: How do you test if a number is strictly divisible by both 3 and 5?
questions.explanation: Both conditions must hold simultaneously, so we use logical AND (&&) with modulus 0: 'number % 3 == 0 && number % 5 == 0'.

questions.prompt: What happens if a semicolon is placed immediately after an if condition: 'if (x > 5);'?
options: The semicolon acts as an empty statement; the following code block executes unconditionally
questions.explanation: A semicolon terminates the statement. 'if (x > 5);' means 'if x > 5, do nothing'. The following block inside { } will run unconditionally regardless of x!
hints: A semicolon acts as an empty body.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: Conditional Thinking

interviewQA.question: Why does Java disallow integers like 0 and 1 in if conditions?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java enforces strict compile-time type safety. In C and C++, `if (count)` or `if (0)` is permitted because non-zero numbers are implicitly treated as boolean truth. However, this causes notorious bugs where assignment (`if (x = 0)`) accidentally compiles. Java eliminates this entire category of bugs by strictly requiring the `boolean` primitive type inside conditional guards.
keyPoints: Strict boolean condition requirement eliminates accidental assignment bugs.

interviewQA.question: What is the accidental assignment bug in boolean conditions, and how does Java handle it?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: If a variable is already boolean (`boolean isReady = false;`), writing `if (isReady = true)` accidentally performs an assignment rather than equality check. In Java, an assignment expression evaluates to the assigned value, so `(isReady = true)` evaluates to `true` and the if block executes! To prevent this, developers can write `if (isReady)` directly, or use tools that flag assignments in conditionals.
keyPoints: if (flag = true) reassigns the boolean and executes; write if (flag) directly.

interviewQA.question: What is the semicolon bug after an if condition: if (condition);?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In Java, a semicolon `;` represents an empty statement. Placing a semicolon immediately after the condition (`if (x > 10);`) causes the if statement to control only that empty statement. Any block of code enclosed in `{ ... }` immediately following it is treated as a standard standalone block and will execute unconditionally every time, creating a silent logic bug.
keyPoints: A semicolon after if condition creates an empty statement, causing the block to run unconditionally.

interviewQA.question: Can an if statement contain another if statement? What is this called?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes, placing an `if` statement inside another `if` block is called a **Nested Condition**. The inner `if` condition is only evaluated if the outer `if` condition evaluated to `true`.
keyPoints: Nested conditions execute inner checks only if outer checks evaluate to true.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between sequential ifs and an if-else chain?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: With sequential independent `if` statements, every single condition is evaluated by the CPU, and multiple blocks can execute if multiple conditions are true. In an `if-else` chain, conditions are mutually exclusive: once a condition evaluates to `true`, its block executes and all subsequent `else-if` and `else` blocks are skipped.
keyPoints: Independent ifs evaluate every condition; if-else chains stop at the first match.

interviewQA.question: What is an early exit or guard clause pattern?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: A guard clause is a conditional check at the very beginning of a method that validates prerequisites (e.g. checking for null, invalid bounds, or unauthenticated users) and exits immediately with `return`. This avoids wrapping the entire method body in deeply nested `if-else` blocks.
keyPoints: Guard clauses check error conditions early and return, keeping the happy path flat and clean.

interviewQA.question: How does branch prediction impact conditional performance in modern CPUs?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: CPUs use pipelined architectures and branch predictors to guess which path an `if` statement will take before the condition is fully evaluated. If the condition pattern is predictable (e.g. sorted arrays), the branch predictor achieves >95% accuracy and zero delay. If the condition is random and unpredictable, branch mispredictions flush the pipeline, causing significant latency.
keyPoints: Branch mispredictions flush the CPU instruction pipeline, causing performance penalties.
